{"id": "2:61/q37", "question": "What does miṣr mean as a place word?", "turns_on": "Boundary and separation, foreign-name, and milking analogies.", "positions": [{"id": "2:61/q37/p1", "position": "A bounded or separated place", "reasons": "MAWARDI-FULL: Others derive miṣr from separating one thing from another. MAWARDI-FULL: A line by ʿAdi ibn Zayd uses miṣran for what separates day and night, as lexical evidence. WAHIDI-BASIT: Misr means a boundary; Adi ibn Zayd's verse makes the sun a boundary between day and night, and the word also means a house's limits or cultivated land separated from wilderness. TABRISI (بعضهم): One etymology derives Miṣr from being cut off from its surroundings by cultivation. TABRISI (آخرون): Another etymology derives Miṣr from its separation from other places. TABRISI (عدي بن زيد): Adi ibn Zayd's verse depicts the sun making Egypt a clear division between day and night, supporting the separation etymology. IBNJAWZI-ZAD (عدي): ʿAdī’s verse uses miṣran to mean a boundary or limit between day and night. IBNJAWZI-ZAD (مفضل الضبي): Al-Mufaḍḍal al-Ḍabbī explains Egypt’s name as the boundary between the eastern and western limits. IBNJAWZI-ZAD: In Hajar usage, miṣr means a place’s boundaries, as in a deed describing a house with its borders. QURTUBI-FULL: Miṣr originally means boundary; miṣr al-dār is the house's limit, and Ibn Fāris says people of Hajar used the term for property boundaries. QURTUBI-FULL (عدي): ʿAdī's line calls the sun a clear boundary dividing day from night, illustrating the root meaning. BAYDAWI-FULL: Miṣr can mean a great city; the word originally denotes a boundary between two things. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (قيل): Miṣr can instead mean a boundary between two lands; Hajar writes bimuṣawrihā for its borders, and the poem depicts the sun as a boundary between day and night. SAMIN-DURR: In the basic language, المصر is the boundary between two things; people of Hajar used مصورها to mean a property's boundaries, and a poem calls the sun a boundary between day and night. ALUSI-FULL: أهبطوا مصرا is a separate reported sentence; it is unjoined because the first is declarative and the second is not, and because descending explains how they could exchange foods. ALUSI-FULL: مصر means a great town and originally denotes a boundary between two things; a quoted poetic line uses it for the boundary dividing day and night."}, {"id": "2:61/q37/p2", "position": "A disputed place-name derivation", "reasons": "MAWARDI-FULL: Some derive miṣr from cutting off, as the city is bounded off by its built-up area. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (الأخفش): Al-Akhfash explains declension despite proper-name and feminine status by the word's lightness from a still middle consonant. BIQAI-FULL: Egypt's name suits its gathering of worldly needs and unusual water; even if it came from a man's name, that coincidence reflects God's knowledge and wisdom over all its details. ALUSI-FULL: Place names can be masculine when considered as places and feminine when considered as lands; if مصر is a feminine town name it takes tanwin because its middle consonant is still."}, {"id": "2:61/q37/p3", "position": "An Arabized foreign name", "reasons": "KASHSHAF-FULL (قيل): One view identifies Egypt with Miṣrāyim, an Arabized form. BAYDAWI-FULL: Another account derives the name from Miṣrātim and says it was Arabized. ALUSI-FULL (قيل): Some derive مصر from the Arabicized Misraim, a son of Noah who first laid out the city; Arabicization permits declension because foreignness no longer governs the form."}, {"id": "2:61/q37/p4", "position": "A name linked to drawing people", "reasons": "IBNJAWZI-ZAD (ابن فارس): Some explain the name Miṣr by people’s intent toward it, like maṣartu al-shāh for milking a sheep because people flock there and rarely leave. ABUHAYYAN-FULL: Miṣr means a city and may derive from milking a sheep completely, drawing everything from its udder. Against — ALUSI-FULL: Deriving the town name from milking every drop from a sheep is far-fetched."}, {"id": "2:61/q37/p5", "position": "A large settled town", "reasons": "BAYDAWI-FULL: Miṣr can mean a great city; the word originally denotes a boundary between two things. ALUSI-FULL: مصر means a great town and originally denotes a boundary between two things; a quoted poetic line uses it for the boundary dividing day and night."}]}
{"id": "2:61/q38", "question": "How is the final rāʾ of miṣran recited?", "turns_on": "Whether tanwīn favors tafkhīm or the preceding vowel favors tarqīq at connection and pause.", "positions": [{"id": "2:61/q38/p1", "position": "Softened rāʾ", "reasons": "NASHR (طاهر بن غلبون): Some authorities, including Ṭāhir b. NASHR (أبو عمرو الداني): Al-Dānī, Abū al-Fatḥ and Ibn Khāqān, Ibn Bulayma, Ibn al-Faḥḥām and al-Shāṭibī soften tanwīn rāʾ in both environments, including after silent yāʾ or adjacent kasra. NASHR (ابن سفيان): Ibn Sufyān and al-Mahdawī instead use tafkhīm in connected recitation because of tanwīn, then tarqīq at pause; this is a second face in al-Kāfī. NASHR (صاحب التبصرة): Al-Tabṣira uniquely reports a second view: a tanwīn rāʾ on the faʿīl pattern is softened at pause but emphatic in connection, attributed to Abū al-Ṭayyib."}, {"id": "2:61/q38/p2", "position": "Emphatic rāʾ", "reasons": "NASHR (طاهر بن غلبون): Some authorities, including Ṭāhir b. NASHR (أبو شامة): Abū Shāma sees no difference between a fatḥa and ḍamma tanwīn rāʾ and says the ḍamma should more strongly favor tafkhīm; the author says al-Jaʿbarī adopted this and wrongly faulted al-Shāṭibī. {"id": "2:61/q39", "question": "How does 'you have what you asked' connect to the command?", "turns_on": "Causal explanation, response to an imperative, or simple sequence marked by fāʾ.", "positions": [{"id": "2:61/q39/p1", "position": "The promise follows the command", "reasons": "MUQATIL: Moses rebuked them for exchanging the inferior produce of the earth for the better manna and quails, and told them to go down to a city where they could obtain what they requested. TAB-FULL (أبو العالية): Abu al-Aliya says their food was quail and their drink manna, and they asked for the produce listed in the verse. TAB-FULL: Al-Tabari supplies the omitted event: Moses prayed, God answered him, and gave the Israelites what they had asked for. BAGHAWI-FULL: What they requested means the plants of the earth. TABRISI: One view says their request was no sin because they asked for another permissible food; Ṭabrisī prefers the view that it was sinful because they rejected God's choice and were reproached. RAZI-FULL: Nothing in the Quran says they were forbidden to request a different food, and the response granting what they asked for indicates the request was permissible; otherwise answering it would entail prophetic sin. QURTUBI-FULL: Third, what God gave them was more delicious than what they requested. QURTUBI-FULL: Mā is the object governed by inna in 'you have what you asked for.' ABUHAYYAN-FULL: The verb has a hamza-root pattern and a wāw-root pattern; يتساولان, analogous to يتجاوبان, supports the latter. ALUSI-FULL: The request is included in the account of blessings: God grants what they asked for by ordering them down to a town, although their ingratitude deserved wrath. IBNASHUR-FULL: The command ‘go down to a town’ is a comparable case where the intended relation is clear without inventing an implicit condition."}, {"id": "2:61/q39/p2", "position": "Promise explains command", "reasons": "BURSEVI: The promise that they will have what they asked for explains the command to descend. ALUSI-FULL: “You will have what you asked” explains the order to descend; al-Bahr instead calls it an answer to the imperative, which can be answered by a clause, with an implied link and pronoun: “therein” and “what you asked for.”"}, {"id": "2:61/q39/p3", "position": "Fāʾ marks sequence after descent", "reasons": "IBNASHUR-FULL: The فاء in فإن لكم ما سألتم marks sequence: they obtain what they requested upon descending, rather than giving a reason for the command. IBNASHUR-FULL: Ibn ʿĀshūr invokes ʿAbd al-Qāhir’s point that إن can itself link and motivate a clause; adding فاء therefore signals simple coordination and sequence."}, {"id": "2:61/q39/p4", "position": "Response to the imperative", "reasons": "ABUHAYYAN-FULL: فإن لكم ما سألتم answers the imperative like a jussive clause; grammarians dispute whether اهبطوا implies a conditional or has an omitted condition."}]}

{"id": "2:61/q43", "question": "When and on whom was the humiliation imposed?", "turns_on": "Whether the condition began in Moses' era, concerns later Jews, or applies to a subset.", "positions": [{"id": "2:61/q43/p1", "position": "Applies to later Jews", "reasons": "WAHIDI-BASIT (جماعة من المفسرين): One reported interpretation takes the humiliation as referring to the people living in Moses’ time; another takes it as referring to people in the Prophet’s time. {"id": "2:61/q44", "question": "How is ʿalayhim pronounced and explained?", "turns_on": "The transmitted hāʾ and mīm vowels and competing original-vowel or harmony analyses.", "positions": [{"id": "2:61/q44/p1", "position": "The pronoun follows transmitted dialects", "reasons": "FARISI-HUJJA: Vowel-following is not always productive analogy: some forms are transmitted, while it is regular in رد، عض، فر and apparently in مردفين. FARISI-HUJJA: Following kasra is already accepted on the mīm of an active-participle marker even though it obscures the pattern, making it still likelier on a pronoun marker. FARISI-HUJJA: Arabic allows vowel-following across an intervening consonant, as in أجوءك for أجيئك and منتن. FARISI-HUJJA: In منحدر, the ḍamma follows the inflectional ḍamma, as in ابنم، امرؤ، أخوك، فوك، and ذو مال. FARISI-HUJJA: أنبؤك can follow the inflectional ḍamma or the initial imperfect-prefix ḍamma, even across an intervening consonant. FARISI-HUJJA (عبد الله بن أبي إسحاق): Abū ʿUthmān reports through Maḥbūb and ʿĪsā that Ibn Abī Isḥāq read بين المرء وقلبه and said رأيت مرءا وهذا مرء. FARISI-HUJJA: The exceptional pronunciation هو يئبى does not refute the pattern because it is anomalous; يخطف has kasra to favor vowel-following. FARISI-HUJJA (أبو الحسن): Abū al-Ḥasan explains يخطف by first kasrating خ for two sukūns, then matching the prefix yāʾ to that kasra. FARISI-HUJJA (أبو الحسن): Abū al-Ḥasan reports from ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar that some Arabs give three-letter nouns beginning with ḍamma a heavy pronunciation. FARISI-HUJJA: Forms of فم show case-conditioned endings (فوك، فاك، فيك); ذو مال behaves similarly but ذو does not take a pronominal suffix. FARISI-HUJJA: With a first-person suffix, فم ends in yāʾ in all cases because the following pronoun imposes kasra, unlike عصاي whose weak ending does not shift with case. FARISI-HUJJA: Following works alike when the triggering vowel is inflectional or built; the distinction does not change the pattern, as ابنم shows. FARISI-HUJJA: The proposal that ابنم’s nūn follows an added mīm is unsound: امرؤ shows the same following without deletion, and مرء is also attested. FARISI-HUJJA: The contrasting forms غد and غدو show that فم’s alternating deletion and completion is not a general consequence of matching وزن. FARISI-HUJJA: Vowel-following has two types: a non-inflectional vowel follows another non-inflectional vowel, as in مغيرة، منتن، يعفر، and ظلمات. FARISI-HUJJA: In the second type, a non-inflectional vowel follows an inflectional one, as in امرؤ، ابنم، فوك، أجوءك، and أنبؤك. FARISI-HUJJA: The examples of فم undermine the claim that these words are inflected in two places; movement can follow either inflection or construction. FARISI-HUJJA: The reversed pattern cited in the grammar book is too rare to establish a rule; comparison of inflection with building is likewise only an exceptional analogy. FARISI-HUJJA: The same principle explains ذال in مذ اليوم: its original ḍamma is retained when the consonant is moved. FARISI-HUJJA: Other readings likewise take more than one dialect form, including variants in أنعام، تكملوا، and يألتكم. FARISI-HUJJA (النبي): A transmitted prophetic report says the Qurʾān was revealed in seven modes, all healing and sufficient. FARISI-HUJJA (نافع): Nāfiʿ is reported to alternate between عليهمو and عليهم, another instance of using both dialect forms. FARISI-HUJJA: Weak radicals remain deleted in forms such as رمت المرأة and لم يخف الرجل despite a vowel inserted for two sukūns; if that vowel counted, forms like لم يقولا would retain the radical. FARISI-HUJJA: The retained yāʾ in لم يكن الذين كفروا is a stronger counterexample because it is frequent and occurs in revelation. FARISI-HUJJA: Poetic deletion can restore an underlying form for metrical necessity, as ضننوا, although ordinary usage keeps the consonant. FARISI-HUJJA: Although the article lām attaches closely and adds definiteness, it behaves like a separate element because it is not part of the word’s root, as in hesitation forms ألي. FARISI-HUJJA: Jussive حذف of nūn in لم يضربا and لم يضربوا shows that transitional movement is not counted like a stable vowel.
